metadata.title: Integrating Randomized Controlled Trials for Drug and Biological Products Into Routine Clinical Practice: Draft Guidance for Industry

Sponsors should consider the complexity of trial requirements, the need for 51 standardization of trial-related activities, and the need for research-specific expertise when 52 deciding on the feasibility of trials in a practice setting. The integration of RCTs into clinical 53 practice should not interfere with the appropriate delivery or administration of patient care. 54

candidates.context: Trials that are most likely to be successfully integrated into clinical practice are those where the 234 data needed for such trials are collected routinely in clinical practice visits with minimal need for 235 protocol-specified procedures or additional visits. It may not be feasible for all trial procedures 236 to be performed by local HCPs during routine care visits, and in these situations, sponsors can 237 consider a hybrid approach, combining data contributed by local HCPs with study-specific 238 procedures performed by trial personnel. 239 IV. candidates.statement: Sponsors must ensure the quality, integrity, and accuracy of the trial data. 23 Sponsors should 254 build appropriate flexibility into trial protocols conducted in whole or in part in clinical practice 255 to accommodate, for example, potential differences in the collection of data in clinical practice or 256 performance of clinical care. This approach can include establishing trial visit windows that 257 largely align with routine clinical practice visits. 258
candidates.context: QbD 22 involves incorporating quality into the design of clinical trials by identifying critical-to- 248 quality factors (i.e., those that are likely to have a meaningful impact on participant’s rights, 249 safety and well-being and the reliability of the results), while eliminating procedures and 250 processes that do not contribute to these primary goals. Simplifying trial designs by using these 251 QbD principles is important for successful integration into clinical practice. 252 22 See the ICH guidance for industry E8(R1) General Considerations for Clinical Studies (April 2022).

candidates.statement: Eligibility criteria are intended to ensure that the trial population has the disease or condition to 277 be studied and that only individuals for whom participation in the trial is safe are enrolled. For 278 trials integrated into clinical practice, eligibility criteria should be minimal and straightforward, 279 without compromising the ability to identify the appropriate population for the trial. Sponsors 280 should attempt to align eligibility criteria with data that are routinely obtained in clinical 281 practice. Eligibility can depend on objective data, including laboratory tests (e.g., 282 microbiological culture, histopathology), physiological tests (e.g., blood pressure, tests of 283 pulmonary function), and/or clinical imaging (e.g., CT scans, radiographs, and echocardiograms) 284 that are routinely collected in clinical practice. Clinical evaluations that are well standardized 285 and unlikely to vary can also be suitable as eligibility criteria. Simple, streamlined criteria that 286 correctly identify the target population can enhance the feasibility and accuracy of enrollment, 287 minimizing randomization of ineligible participants. 288

candidates.statement: Drugs that are already FDA-approved for an intended use have better established safety profiles 313 and are generally more suitable for use in trials integrated into clinical practice than drugs that 314 are unapproved for any use. An approved product’s well-characterized safety profile for the 315 approved use may mean that limited collection of safety data for the unapproved use may be 316 appropriate in certain circumstances. For example, when using an FDA-approved drug, it may 317 be appropriate to consider selective collection of safety data, such as serious adverse events, 318 adverse events of special interest, and adverse events that lead to discontinuation of the drug or 319 withdrawal from the trial without the need to collect nonserious adverse events that are already 320 well characterized. 29 , 30 Sponsors should consult with the relevant FDA review division to 321 determine whether a selective approach to safety data collection would be appropriate. 322
